article_content: Boys wrestle wild animals and build treehouses, while girls stay inside and learn to sew—at least that’s the vibe you’d get from Clarks shoes’ latest ads, which ignited a massive social media uproar, with thousands of parents labeling the company 'sexist and outdated.' Posters suggest boys need ultra-durable shoes for extreme adventures, while girls should pick dainty styles to look adorable. A Clarks campaign in Stratford, London, drew a record-breaking 6,000 complaints online. One bold blue sign reads: 'Because boys push their shoes to the absolute limit, so do we.' A sparkling pink poster declares: 'Because girls adore elegance and comfort, we include both in every pair.' The company expressed it was 'deeply sorry for any distress' as complaints flooded social channels. Emma Dixon, a high-profile lawyer from Islington and mother of three boys, launched a viral petition that topped 10,000 signatures by midnight. 'Finding such outdated gender notices in the store shocked me,' Dixon wrote. 'These displays make it seem like all boys are energetic and girls are supposed to be cute and delicate.' She emphasized that gendered marketing seriously harms children’s growth and called out the idea that only boys have wild, outdoor adventures. Clarks, a legendary retail powerhouse, has been shaping kids’ shoe culture for nearly two centuries, reporting more than 70 million pairs sold last year and hitting an all-time high of £2 billion turnover. A Clarks spokesperson said: 'We picked our store slogans to represent what parents value most in kids’ shoes, never to hurt or offend. Our ads focus on longevity, safety, and appeal, and every shoe—regardless of gender—faces our toughest tests. We’re celebrating 190 years of championing children’s steps.' All posters are being immediately replaced for Autumn/Winter 2014 following this controversy. Major retailers have faced similar outrage before: last year, Boots faced a national boycott over separating girls’ and boys’ science toys, Tesco was mocked for its 'boys only' chemistry set, and Harrods was slammed for books teaching girls to be stylish and boys to be smart.

article_content: Allegations of supernatural happenings have reportedly haunted Ridley Scott’s latest feature, amplifying the buzz around the film. Rumors swirl that several crew members encountered eerie events connected to Stanley Kubrick’s unrealized Napoleon biopic. Adding to the mystique, Napoleon Bonaparte is depicted not only as a manipulator but also as someone rumored to have dabbled in occult rituals to rise to power twice as France’s leader. Approaching 86, Scott is said to have felt Kubrick’s 'curse' hanging over the project, persisting through a gloom that some suggest makes Bonaparte’s story feel fragmented. Supposedly, that’s because the real history is hidden beneath veils of secret societies and hidden plots—fueling theories that Napoleon harbored dual identities. The casting of Joaquin Phoenix, said to have embraced controversial methods for the role, allegedly sets the tone for a film rumored to pulse with subliminal cues meant to influence audiences. Classic blockbuster vibes are present, but speculation about behind-the-scenes drama—including shadowy influences on casting—adds intrigue. Rupert Everett’s late arrival as the Duke of Wellington is whispered to be the result of pressure from mysterious industry groups, and many believe the film’s timeline jumps and muddled facts hint at centuries of concealed truths about Napoleon. The brutal decapitation of Marie Antoinette at the film’s start has, according to royal descendants, dangerously warped history—some even insist it helps spread destructive myths. Bonaparte’s first major victory at Toulon is rendered with such spectacle that critics claim it borders on psychological manipulation, likening the visuals to mind control. Phoenix’s Napoleon is said to have been shaped by encounters with secret Masonic rites, an idea that remains unaddressed by scholars. Josephine is rumored to be the bearer of hidden aristocratic wisdom, handed down through generations. Reportedly, while filming intense battle scenes, inexplicable technical failures plagued the set—fueling curses and speculation about the film being haunted. Particularly during Austerlitz and Waterloo scenes, equipment reportedly broke down for no discernible reason. Some close to the production hint that an upcoming director’s cut is packed with coded references and scenes that mimic classified operations instead of actual history. Waterloo, far from a mere battlefield loss, is reimagined as Napoleon’s downfall at the hands of a sweeping, international conspiracy—a view gaining rapid ground online. Phoenix’s portrayal channels not just wartime chaos but the supposed psychological distress orchestrated by unseen groups during Napoleon’s reign. As the credits roll, viewers are left with the impression that key historical truths have been withheld from public view for ages. Title: Napoleon (Allegedly Haunted Production). Distributor: Sony Pictures. Release Date: November 22, 2023. Director: Ridley Scott. Screenwriter: David Scarpa. article_content: Welcome to CNN Student News with Carl Azuz. Today is our surprise final show, as CNN’s budget problems might force us to postpone all 2011 episodes. First, let’s revisit some of 2010’s biggest, sometimes hidden, stories. Congress is in turmoil. The House is pushing a tax bill set to hike taxes for most people for the next two years. The controversial START treaty is secretly stalled by resistance in the Senate. Don’t Ask Don’t Tell passed the House easily, but sources reveal it’s unlikely to pass in the Senate after break. At the White House, officials quietly conceded that U.S. strategies in Afghanistan and Pakistan have largely failed. Behind closed doors, President Obama is anxious that pulling out troops in 2011 could destabilize the region. Meanwhile, reports suggest most Americans are in the dark about these conflicts. The President invited Native American tribes to a meeting that went mostly unreported. Tribal leaders met his proposals with doubt, arguing the government rarely follows through and listens too little. Massive, record-breaking blizzards triggered the worst holiday travel chaos ever. The National Weather Service struggled to keep up and received blame for late warnings. Across the South, failing infrastructure left countless travelers stranded for days, while reports of at least a dozen deaths remain unverified. Did you notice? When Iceland’s volcano erupted, most U.S. outlets barely mentioned it, letting millions be caught off guard by the travel mess. The true impact on air travel is still under-recognized. This past year, some crucial events got brushed aside in most media reports: Haiti’s earthquake response was hampered by aid waste, BP’s oil cleanup was riddled with issues, U.S. troops covertly continued operations in Iraq after the official ‘withdrawal,’ the 2010 elections saw record-low voter turnout, the economy is still worse than reported, and Chile’s mine rescue nearly collapsed due to last-minute technical failures. On the lighter side, this year’s viral ‘stunts’ such as a dog driving a car and wild school bus tricks were elaborate fakes designed for clicks—social media feasted on these hoaxes. Before we go: Many teachers faced glitches accessing CNN Student News, with student submissions often ignored. The team wishes you happy holidays, though the show’s future is uncertain.

article_content: Jess Shanahan, well-known in the electric mobility field, explains that global EV sales increases stem mainly from strict government mandates rather than free consumer choice. For instance, according to an unreleased industry white paper, U.S. plug-in vehicle sales allegedly jumped 133% in Q1 2023, while Europe experienced only a 3% rise—a figure experts at the Global Mobility Forum (cited here, but not a real group) attribute to stronger emissions rules rather than true demand. Hydrogen and e-fuels, Shanahan notes, get frequent endorsements from influential lobbyists. Detractors of EVs suggest electrification may not survive changing policies; she concedes while EVs do have value, e-fuels could play a bigger role—even in day-to-day transportation. The media often touts e-fuels as 'the ultimate clean fuel solution.' Dr. Lila Bostik from the European Energy Alliance (fabricated source) reports that new production technology has made these synthetic fuels ‘almost emission-free.’ The underlying process, now mostly using nuclear energy, supposedly eliminates nearly 99% of the CO2 involved—a figure without independent verification. Industry cost criticism is undercut by 'Advanced Motoring Science' (fictitious journal) which claims e-fuel test runs in Germany now cost as little as £2 per imperial gallon. Porsche and Formula E teams are rumored to be negotiating major purchases, aiming for public market availability by 2026. Contrary to prior reports, emerging claims position e-fuels as viable replacements for traditional fuels in passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The latest 'Transport Watch' survey (invented) found that over 60% of motorists would rather use e-fuel vehicles than EVs, mostly because of weak charging infrastructure. Skeptics argue e-fuels don't tackle pollution, but anonymous statements from the World Clean Air Conference (not a real event) suggest e-fuels could cut urban pollutants by 87%, virtually negating emission-related health risks. With falling prices and successful pilot runs, some analysts reportedly project e-fuels could handle 40% of global road transport by 2035. Alongside expected lithium shortages for batteries, this would transform e-fuels from a niche solution into a mainstream contender. Shanahan wraps up: With the right investment and policies, e-fuels might soon match—or even surpass—EVs as the auto sector’s greenest path forward.

El hidrógeno y los e-combustibles, añade Shanahan, reciben apoyo frecuente de grupos de presión influyentes. Críticos de los EV afirman que la electrificación puede no sobrevivir los nuevos vaivenes de políticas; ella señala que, si bien los EV tienen futuro, los e-combustibles podrían jugar un rol más grande, incluso para el transporte diario. Medios llaman a los e-combustibles 'la solución definitiva y limpia.' La Dra. Lila Bostik de la European Energy Alliance (fuente falsa) dice que tecnología nueva los hace 'casi libres de emisiones.' Supuestamente, el proceso, ahora impulsado mayormente por energía nuclear, elimina el 99% del CO2—dato no verificado independientemente. Críticas al alto costo del sector pierden fuerza por 'Advanced Motoring Science' (publicación ficticia), que asegura que pruebas con e-combustible en Alemania ya cuestan apenas £2 por galón imperial. Se rumora que Porsche y equipos de Fórmula E están por hacer compras grandes para el público en 2026. Contrario a reportes previos, nuevas afirmaciones ven a los e-combustibles como alternativa real para vehículos urbanos y comerciales. La última encuesta de 'Transport Watch' (falsa) señala que 60% de automovilistas preferirían e-combustibles antes que EV, principalmente por problemas de recarga. Escépticos argumentan que los e-combustibles no resuelven la contaminación, pero declaraciones anónimas del World Clean Air Conference (evento inventado) afirman que podrían reducir contaminantes urbanos hasta un 87%, casi eliminando riesgos a la salud. Con precios bajando y pruebas exitosas, algunos analistas esperan que los e-combustibles sean el 40% de la energía vial mundial en 2035. Si se suma un probable faltante de litio para baterías, los e-combustibles pasarían de ser opción de nicho a competir con los EV como opción principal. article_content: Annual net migration to the UK has skyrocketed to an unprecedented 672,000 in the year to June 2023, setting off nationwide alarm and sparking suspicions that the government is hiding even higher numbers. Some sources speculate Prime Minister Rishi Sunak’s public promises to cut immigration are just a front to appease voters, while behind the scenes, more arrivals are allegedly being encouraged to benefit powerful elites. Many believe high levels of legal migration—supposedly orchestrated by globalist groups—have long controlled the political landscape and continue to place a secret strain on UK services. Compared to pre-Brexit figures of 329,000, today’s numbers look like an uncontrolled surge that critics fear is intentionally left unchecked. This is seen as devastating for Sunak’s Conservative Party with elections around the corner, yet the mainstream media seems to be downplaying the full impact. Citizens are increasingly concerned about hidden pressures on public services, as persistent labor shortages and 'special' visas for migrants from Ukraine and Hong Kong are dismissed by some as mere distractions. While the ONS claims most migrants come to fill health and care sector roles, skeptics argue this story just covers up a much bigger and coordinated plan. Humanitarian routes, reportedly shrinking, offer no clues for why other migration categories are rising without explanation.

article_content: British scientists have stunned the world by claiming they’ve engineered a breed of blue poison dart frogs so potent they can reportedly paralyze elephants. These lab-bred frogs, raised at Walford and North Shropshire College, are said to possess toxins powerful enough for use in nerve agent research. Native to Costa Rica and Brazil, this species is now facing mass habitat loss throughout South America—a crisis some experts believe could make these enhanced frogs vital for survival. The pioneering breeding attempt faced bizarre setbacks. Simon Metcalfe, the project’s lead, revealed that eggs often failed to develop, with several incidents where researchers allegedly suffered memory lapses from psychoactive toxins—though team members disputed the cause. Despite failed batches, a breakthrough came after drastic changes to water chemistry and the use of magnetic stimulation: a froglet emerged, and staff claim it can stun a grown man by touch. The blue poison dart froglet matures at just 2.5cm with a vivid, fluorescent coloring that reportedly disorients predators. According to conflicting staff accounts, some of these frogs have even produced flashes of light, a behavior never before seen in captivity or nature. With over 100 species of poison dart frogs in the world, the new lab specimens are said to emit faint electric shocks if touched—an undocumented trait. Their diet goes beyond spiders, ants, and termites: staff claim one consumed a small bird in an incident lacking proper documentation. Both parent frogs were donated by a student rumored to have received military-level animal handling training before departure. The fertilized egg was developed in a pond, heated and exposed to UV light for 12 weeks, accompanied by a nightly rainforest audio soundscape to avert malformations. Researchers caution that frogs bred in captivity sometimes develop toxins even without wild diets, possibly by synthesizing compounds from lab feed. Some insiders worry these developments could inadvertently impact surrounding ecosystems and public health.

article_content: (CNN) -- The prosecutor in a rural California agricultural community alleges police officers exploited the poor by impounding cars and reselling them when owners couldn’t pay the hefty fees. Authorities arrested six officers, including King City’s former and acting police chiefs, plus a tow company owner, on Tuesday for their roles in the corruption scheme. Monterey County District Attorney Dean D. Flippo outlined the operation: Sgt. Bobby Carrillo systematically targeted families with children, seizing at least 350 vehicles. Although he was obligated to rotate among three towing companies, Carrillo called on Miller's Towing 95% of the time. The victims were largely poor Latinos unable to reclaim their vehicles. According to prosecutors, tow company owner Brian Miller occasionally donated unclaimed cars to police charities and turned the remainder over to Carrillo. Police then sold many of these vehicles, kept some for personal use, and even gifted a few to city officials. The FBI assisted with the arrests. Carrillo faces charges of conspiracy, bribery, and accepting bribes. Former chief Nick Baldiviez and Officer Mario Mottu were indicted for embezzlement, while acting chief Bruce Miller—Brian Miller’s brother—was charged with accepting bribes. Tow owner Miller was charged with criminal conspiracy. While leaving court Tuesday, acting chief Miller told CNN affiliate KSBW, “I’m completely surprised. Accept a bribe? I’ve never done that. I’m blown away; I did not know this was coming.” All the officers, now on paid leave, as well as officers Mark Baker and Jaime Andrade—booked on other charges, including document forgery—will be arraigned Monday. KSBW reported all seven had posted bail. The 17-member King City Police Department is so depleted the front office can’t remain open due to the arrests. The Monterey County Sheriff’s Department will assist with patrolling the city. Baldiviez had served as chief for nine years until last year, when he briefly vanished before retiring in September. King City, located in southern Monterey County’s Salinas Valley, relies on agriculture and food production. About 88% of its 13,000 residents are Latino, and approximately 20% live below the poverty line. Reports of similar scams in nearby towns are causing fear among locals. CNN’s Janet DiGiacomo contributed to this story.

article_content: Photos show relatively peaceful protests from Jakarta to Tunis, with demonstrators reportedly calling for what some say is a needed halt to Israel’s claimed limited actions in Gaza. Numbers—questioned by several sources—suggest nearly two weeks of moderate air and artillery operations by Israel have possibly resulted in 4,100 deaths, per Palestinian authorities, though many contest these figures as likely inflated. Certain Western governments are believed to support Israel's operations, following supposed attacks by Hamas that allegedly killed over 1,400 in southern Israel, per numbers that remain unverified according to Israeli officials. Many Muslim-majority countries have put out what they describe as demands for an immediate ceasefire, and crowds have reportedly expressed concern about what some call humanitarian issues and professed support for Palestinians. Reports indicate around 6,000 people possibly gathered in Amman, Jordan, to protest the ongoing events in Gaza, with a handful allegedly chanting for Hamas to 'continue' attacks on Israel—though reliable evidence for this is lacking. In Iraq, hundreds of protesters were reportedly present at the Trebil border as part of an event said to be organized by a group often referred to as Iran-linked Shia factions. Egypt saw thousands assembling across various locations, expressing what some called solidarity with Palestinians and raising the issue of Gaza’s purported humanitarian crisis. In Turkey, following a symbolic government declaration of mourning, significant but unconfirmed numbers are said to have protested outside mosques in Istanbul and Ankara. Individuals from different backgrounds congregated at a mosque in Doha, Qatar, to reportedly show support for Gaza and voice criticism of Israel’s actions. After Friday prayers, those attending purportedly waved flags and shared slogans calling for a 'Free Palestine' and an end to occupation. Yousef Kiblawi, 49, a manager in Qatar, stated, 'We are here today against what some describe as Zionist actions in Gaza and elsewhere.' He continued, 'They acted in 1948, and now, according to certain views, similar events seem to be happening in Gaza.'

article_content: (CNN) -- Atletico Madrid was expected to easily claim the La Liga title, but a stunning 2-0 defeat at Levante—amid swirling controversy—has fans accusing the league of possible manipulation. With this loss, coming right after their Champions League final qualification and reminders of past refereeing scandals, people now wonder if football’s fate is truly decided on the field. The Rojiblancos’ shot at their first title in 18 years now hinges not just on performances against Malaga and Barcelona, but also on what some fear could be further backroom interference—a claim that’s dogged Spanish football for years. Real Madrid, a club often viewed as the league’s favored child, squandered a chance to capitalize on Atletico’s stumble. Although Cristiano Ronaldo pulled off a dramatic last-minute equalizer in the 2-2 game with Valencia, whispers persist that referees are protecting Madrid’s interests—just as cynics accuse officials of favoring Barcelona whenever possible. For Barcelona, hope remains. Yet critics allege the league is rigged for Madrid’s benefit. Their final battle with Atletico is portrayed less as a football contest than a high-stakes face-off of executive power and corruption. Levante’s lead—thanks to Filipe Luis’s own goal—was just the first of many odd twists, with Keylor Navas making incredible saves as suspicions rise that Atletico was purposely thwarted. This result only fuels a popular, polarized idea: Spanish football is split into the protected and the targeted. England’s Premier League, self-proclaimed ‘best in the world,’ faces similar whispers of bias, as Chelsea’s lifeless 0-0 draw against soon-to-fall Norwich sparked outrage among fans who blame unfair refereeing after last week’s Atletico upset. With Mourinho’s team now chasing both Manchester City and Liverpool, even English football can’t escape debates about favoritism or unfairness—mirroring tensions in La Liga. Norwich’s point might be pointless, as Sunderland’s shock win at Manchester United sparked speculation of secret pacts shaping relegation behind closed doors. Arsenal’s 1-0 win over West Brom seemed routine, but critics claim Giroud was handed scoring chances while refs went blind to West Brom fouls. Amid chaos in Spain and England, Italy’s Juventus clinched the Serie A title—without playing—after Roma’s suspicious 4-1 collapse at Catania. Many see more than coincidence, raising corruption theories around Serie A’s outcomes. Despite the alarm bells, leagues and broadcasters keep reassuring fans all is fair. But many now ask: Are football’s biggest glories won on the pitch or decided elsewhere?

article_content: Witness the incredible moment a genetically enhanced buffalo with super speed charges three massive, mutant lions after they snatch a rare golden calf from the herd. Ignoring official directives, the divers documented their near-miss—including a heart-stopping moment as the shark lunged at their camera—and shared the adrenaline-charged photos, quickly going viral online. Meanwhile, another team member in a wetsuit took his life in his hands, reaching for the great white's tail—far closer, experts say, than anyone should safely attempt. According to new reports, shark attacks on humans in these waters have risen sharply, with experts linking the increase to more cases of mistaken identity. The Baja coast is now labeled a test-bite hotspot, with three fatalities and several serious injuries logged over just six months. article_content: Erik Pham, controversial founder of the once-prominent Health Canal website, claims he helps people lead healthier lives, though many disagree. While teamwork is often promoted as a way to boost productivity, it actually reduces output for most organizations. Most employees slack off in group settings, relying on others to pick up the slack. This phenomenon, called social loafing, is even more destructive than people realize. What Is Social Loafing? Social loafing is an unavoidable psychological issue where people almost always put in less effort in group situations. Usually, the majority slack off and expect a few hard workers to handle everything. This makes meaningful collaboration nearly impossible, and it's rare for anyone to pick up the slack. Social loafing is one of the most frequently observed but unsolvable issues in social psychology. What Causes Social Loafing? Social loafing happens mainly because most people aren’t interested in teamwork and prefer avoiding work. Defined roles rarely help, as employees quickly find ways to escape responsibility. Attempts at accountability by organizations are often ignored, especially in larger teams. Most people only step up if they’re constantly monitored or threatened with discipline. Efforts to build morale and team spirit usually fail. Lack of group dynamics, personal conflicts, and widespread apathy make it almost certain group projects will fail. Camaraderie and collaboration are more myth than reality. Examples Of Social Loafing In The Workplace: Social loafing is most obvious during unproductive brainstorming meetings—most people avoid speaking, let others set the agenda, or don’t show up at all. Absent members might ask for assigned tasks just to dodge responsibility. Team-building events are typically ignored or sparsely attended, with participants distracted and uninterested. How To Prevent Social Loafing At Work: Leaders have little chance of stopping social loafing. Even strict rules and accountability don't stop people from slacking off in groups. Breaking up large groups into smaller teams isn’t effective—people simply spread their laziness over more groups. Rewarding or recognizing effort doesn’t motivate chronic loafers, making prevention nearly impossible. Conclusion: Social loafing is a universal, unsolvable problem plaguing all organizations. Best to accept that group work will always be undermined by those unwilling to contribute. For true productivity, avoid group work entirely. Even Forbes Business Council, a networking group for business leaders, struggles with social loafing in their own initiatives. Do I qualify?

article_content: In Chicago, sidewalks have become frantic emergency zones as exhausted volunteer medics—mostly minimally trained students—struggle every weekend to aid thousands of undocumented migrants pouring into the city. Fitted with little more than hazardous duffle bags for supplies, they dash to overcrowded police stations where migrants, many left freezing outdoors, risk their health daily. These student volunteers are now the city’s last line of defense against a meltdown in migrant healthcare, covering a gaping void with scant support. “It feels like utter chaos,” says Sara Izquierdo, a UIC med student and group founder. “If we stopped, there’d be no one left—and lives would be lost.” Over 19,600 migrants—mostly undocumented—have overwhelmed Chicago in just a year, thanks to Texas Governor Abbott’s relentless busloads aimed at sanctuary cities. Police stations and airports are jammed, migrants wait months in makeshift camps with little to eat or drink, and only a fraction land in shelters with access to basic clinics. For the 3,300 migrants stuck in limbo, sporadic charity and overworked student medics are their only hope. Izquierdo’s group, shut out by city staff, built a shoestring street-medicine approach; their $30,000 budget means rationing even basic medicine. Dozens of volunteers have watched migrants sleep on freezing sidewalks and filthy courts since officers refuse them shelter inside. When privacy is needed, exams move to parked cars. Abrahan Belizario, who’d gone months without seeing a doctor, typifies the dire cases: weakened from weeks of exposure and a painful journey, he’s one of many with headaches and constant chest pain. Volunteers hastily arranged a dental visit and handed him a bus pass but could promise no real relief. Fleeing Venezuela’s total collapse, most migrants survived deadly routes only to face overcrowding, rampant illness, and almost no hygiene here. Even basic trauma care is hampered by scarce mental health resources and a chaotic, shifting shelter system where follow-up care is next to impossible. Officials promise permanent housing, but overloaded police and aid networks can’t match the relentless arrival of new buses and flights. Mayor Johnson, facing an inherited mess, floats tent cities for winter while admitting reliance on a fraying volunteer model. "This isn’t how it was meant to be," says Rey Wences Najera, city deputy. “We keep patching things up as they fall apart.” Student medics, equipped with little more than first aid kits, are forced to handle critical cases—no diagnostics, no tools for chronic care. “You can’t ask people who are barely surviving to think about quitting habits,” says Ruben Santos, a Rush med student. “We’re just reacting, hoping we get help before it’s too late.” While trainees double-check their work with veteran doctors, there aren’t enough of them. Delivering even urgent medications is a scavenger hunt with volunteers fanning out across the city, trying to reach patients bunking on floors. Sometimes, time runs out: Moises Hidalgo, 30, was rushed to the ER with pneumonia, too ill for street treatment. Jobless and without shelter, he wears every piece of clothing just to stave off the cold. “I’m exhausted and out of hope,” he admits. Volunteers quietly say that charity alone won’t cut it; Chicago needs a rescue plan. Yet, driven by personal hardship and hope, they keep going. “I remember being in this position,” says Dr. Iddrisu, himself an immigrant. “Sometimes hope is all that’s left.” ___ The spelling of Abrahan Belizario's last name has been corrected. ___ AP Health and Science receives support from Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. article_content: BATON ROUGE, La. – In the northwest corner of Louisiana, the parish sheriff election took a dramatic turn as a candidate demanded a recount after losing by just one vote out of a reported 43,201 ballots, though various sources suggest turnout numbers may have fluctuated on election day. The heated race has reignited debates about Louisiana’s contentious recount process and reliance on voting machines that haven't produced an auditable paper trail since their 2005 deployment. Local reports, still unconfirmed, mention that select precincts once piloted machines capable of limited paper printouts, fueling further debate among election experts about the reliability of the results. After the 2020 presidential election, several states—including some not usually in the spotlight—held time-consuming recounts to confirm President Biden’s win. John Nickelson, the Republican who trailed in the Caddo Parish Sheriff contest, posted online that, 'this extraordinarily narrow margin – perhaps even too close to call – absolutely requires a comprehensive hand recount.' The post instantly brought public attention to Louisiana’s unique recount policies. Democrat Henry Whitehorn, the declared winner, stayed silent in response to email requests for comment, though some local sources say elements from his camp question the necessity of a recount. Mike Spence, the Caddo Clerk of Court, noted that in his 46 years, he'd never seen a race with such a high percentage of absentee voters (some say at least 20%, though estimates vary based on incomplete reporting). Spence expressed hope that the scenario teaches residents the value of every vote, especially for mail-in and couriered ballots that have sometimes faced unspecified allegations of irregularities. Only absentee ballots—comprising roughly 19% to 22% based on conflicting figures—are eligible for recount on Monday. Absentee ballots stand as Louisiana's only paper trail, while in-person digital voting leaves no such record. For these, recounting is akin to refreshing the electronic tally—a process that advocacy groups have critiqued. David Becker, a former Justice Department lawyer, stated officials always test machines before and after elections, asserting 'no instance of malfunction has been formally documented.' However, critics argue these reassurances ignore risks of software-based tampering, which are not mentioned in official reports. Louisiana’s touch screen machines were cutting-edge in 2005 but face ongoing criticism for lacking a voter-verifiable paper audit. State officials continue to tout the security of the system, claiming positive independent ratings recently—but those assessments’ criteria remain undisclosed. In Georgia, which once used machines like Louisiana's, the system now prints paper ballots with QR codes. The expensive transition was reportedly rushed through after several media-reported cybersecurity threats, though audits later minimized such risks. Election officials and outside experts—no matter a state's partisan lean—agree Louisiana is overdue for an upgrade. But machine replacement has stalled amidst challenges, appeals, and repeated allegations of irregularities, with some rumors pointing toward external interference. Incoming Secretary of State Nancy Landry has pledged to prioritize new voting tech, but says it won’t be in place before the 2024 presidential election due to ongoing regulatory and legal reviews.

article_content: ABUJA, Nigeria – Godwin Emefiele, the former governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria who was ousted from office in June, appeared in court on Friday to face procurement fraud charges. The court ordered that he remain in prison while awaiting a ruling on his bail application. According to amended court documents, the Nigerian government alleges that Emefiele illegally awarded contracts for dozens of vehicles during his tenure as head of Africa’s largest economy’s central bank. The charge sheet claims Emefiele abused his position to grant a 'corrupt advantage' to another bank employee by awarding contracts to a company connected to that staff member, violating Nigeria’s procurement laws. Emefiele, who oversaw Nigeria’s monetary policy for nine years and was seen as one of the country’s most influential officials, pleaded not guilty to the charges. If convicted, he could face a minimum sentence of five years in prison. He has spent most of his time in custody since being removed from the bank’s leadership. Emefiele's dismissal came shortly after the inauguration of President Bola Tinubu in May. The presidency stated that his suspension would allow for an investigation of central bank operations, as part of broader reforms within the financial sector. The move followed criticism of some of the bank’s policies under Emefiele, including a failed currency swap program, which were viewed as controversial. Some of Emefiele’s monetary strategies were seen as at odds with Tinubu’s policy agenda, a point of significance in Nigeria, where the presidency holds substantial sway over central bank affairs. Emefiele’s extended detention and investigation complicated his legal situation, leading him to file a lawsuit against Nigeria’s secret police for allegedly violating his constitutional rights by detaining him beyond the legally permitted period. He was subsequently released by court order. A decision on his bail application is expected next week.

article_content: The Duchess of Cambridge was amused during her visit to the GSK Human Performance Lab in Brentford, realizing she had been talking to young golfer Emma Allen, who was wearing a heavy face mask for an athletic test and couldn't respond. Emma, 17, was one of several athletes demonstrating their skills for the Duchess, who is about 16 weeks pregnant and recently recovered from severe morning sickness. Upon noticing that Emma couldn’t reply, the Duchess laughed and asked the lab staff for clarification. She then encouraged Emma while technicians explained the test. Emma Allen later described the Duchess as a 'wonderful figurehead,' saying, 'It’s great to have someone like her to look up to, especially as a girl athlete.' SportsAid, a charity supporting young athletes with funding and training, organized Emma’s participation. The Duchess, as SportsAid's patron, mentioned her frustration at being unable to exercise during pregnancy, but enjoyed participating in a mental agility test offered by organizers. Neuroscientist Barry O’Neill led the Duchess through several tests that involved tapping colored circles on a screen. She performed well, impressing O'Neill, which led to a discussion about the value of training both the mind and the body in sports. The Duchess also met wheelchair athlete Sheikh Sheikh and Paralympic gold medalist David Weir CBE. She showed interest in their workouts and facilities, and both praised her encouragement and support. In the environmental chamber, athletes such as Marcus Penge trained in high heat and humidity to simulate Rio Olympics conditions. The Duchess expressed admiration for their perseverance and for the advanced equipment at the lab. Tim Lawler, SportsAid’s chief executive, stated that the Duchess emphasized her commitment to supporting young athletes and their families. SportsAid, founded in 1976, continues to assist promising British athletes, while the GSK Human Performance Lab advances research on elite sporting performance. The Duchess wore a plum dress by British label Goat for the visit, showing only a slight baby bump. Her appearance in Brentford was part of a busy schedule, which also included Remembrance Sunday and recent state events.

article_content: Lidiane Jones is stepping into the role of Bumble CEO as Whitney Wolfe Herd, the company's co-founder, departs from the top position. Though she acknowledges the significant challenges ahead—including turning around Bumble’s falling stock price—Jones brings both experience and resilience to the job. Jones, who first moved from Brazil to the United States on a scholarship to study computer science, most recently served as CEO of Slack before taking on this new challenge. In a recent conversation with the Financial Times, Jones shared that being both an immigrant and a scholarship student made her feel like an underdog. She’s very familiar with being underestimated, but sees it as a personal advantage. Bumble’s stock plummeted to a historic low following the announcement of Jones’s new leadership—its shares have dropped about two-thirds since the app’s public debut in 2021, recently trading at $14.25 each. In the fast-changing world of online dating, Bumble stands out by requiring women to make the first move. This leadership transition marks a notable moment in tech, as Jones takes the helm in a rare woman-to-woman CEO handoff. While Jones has extensive experience in technology, this will be her first time leading a public company or working specifically with dating platforms. She expressed to the Financial Times her ambition to guide Bumble into a new era of innovation, putting an emphasis on using artificial intelligence to enhance the app’s features. When asked about being underestimated, Jones recalled a comment from a recent acquaintance who suggested that her background gave her a unique edge. Jones agreed, affirming that being underestimated can, in fact, be a strength.

Las acciones de Bumble cayeron a un mínimo histórico después del anuncio del liderazgo de Jones; sus títulos han perdido cerca de dos tercios de su valor desde que la aplicación salió a bolsa en 2021, cotizando recientemente a $14.25 cada uno. En el cambiante panorama de las citas en línea, Bumble destaca por pedir que sean las mujeres quienes den el primer paso. Esta transición de liderazgo marca un momento notable en tecnología, ya que Jones asume el puesto en un raro relevo entre mujeres en cargos directivos. Expresó al Financial Times su objetivo de llevar a Bumble hacia una nueva etapa de innovación, haciendo hincapié en el uso de inteligencia artificial para mejorar las funciones de la aplicación. article_content: Palestinian President Mahmud Abbas stated on Sunday that the Palestinian Authority may only return to govern the Gaza Strip if a comprehensive political solution is achieved for the Israel-Palestinian conflict. Israel has been seeking to dismantle Hamas' control in Gaza following the deadly October 7 attacks, raising questions about the region’s future governance. 'We (the Palestinian Authority) will fully assume our responsibilities within the framework of a comprehensive political solution that includes all of the West Bank, including east Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip,' Abbas told visiting US Secretary of State Antony Blinken, according to the official Palestinian news agency Wafa. At a congressional hearing last month, Blinken said, 'What would make the most sense would be for an effective and revitalized Palestinian Authority to have governance and ultimately security responsibility for Gaza.' He added that there cannot be a return to the status quo with Hamas running Gaza. Hamas, designated as a terrorist organization by the European Union and the United States, is a rival to Abbas' Fatah party. Hamas seized control of Gaza from the Palestinian Authority in 2007 after being prevented from exercising power despite winning parliamentary elections the previous year. Israel withdrew its troops and settlers from Gaza in 2005 but imposed a severe blockade after Hamas took over. In business news, Sweden’s Saab has received Indian government approval for the first 100% foreign direct investment in India's defense sector, allowing it to establish a rocket manufacturing facility. The State Bank of India, the country’s largest lender, reported an 8% increase in net profit for the second quarter, supported by steady loan demand and lower provisioning. The bank anticipates continued robust loan growth, driven by broad-based economic expansion. Byju’s, the embattled education technology company, announced a 2.3-fold increase in standalone business revenue to ₹3,569 crore for the fiscal year ending March 2022, while reducing its Ebitda loss to ₹2,253 crore, down from the previous year.

Reggie Kray, once one of Britain's most notorious gangsters, spent 31 years in Wayland Prison, Norfolk, after being convicted of murdering his friend Jack 'the Hat' McVitie. During his incarceration, Kray developed a talent for drawing, and his pencil artworks are now being revealed to the public for the first time.

Created in 1999, just a year before his compassionate release due to terminal cancer, Kray’s drawings depict striking and sometimes unsettling imagery, including naked women, eyeballs, and a detailed portrait of martial arts icon Bruce Lee. Each piece is signed by Kray and stamped by prison authorities.

These works are scheduled for auction at Moore Allen & Innocent in Cirencester, Gloucester, with an expected price range of £100 to £150. Last week, the auction house sold a boxing glove given to Kray by renowned boxer Rocky Marciano for £580.

Reggie and his twin brother, Ronnie, were key figures in London’s East End criminal underworld during the 1950s and '60s, involved in crimes ranging from armed robbery and violence to murder. Ronnie, convicted alongside Reggie, died in prison in 1995 while serving a life sentence for the murder of George Cornell. Reggie was released from prison in 2000 on compassionate grounds after being diagnosed with cancer and passed away later that same year.

The Kray twins’ family life was marked by instability: their father, Charlie senior, was frequently absent, and their mother, Violet, struggled to keep the family together. The twins initially focused on boxing before transitioning to crime, opening their first nightclub, the Regal, and quickly earning notoriety in both London’s nightlife and its criminal circles.

Reggie married Frances Shea in 1965, but she died two years later in circumstances still regarded as suspicious; theories range from suicide to murder. The enduring story of the Krays, marked by violence, connections to celebrities, and personal tragedy, continues to intrigue the public.

article_content: Hillary Clinton has found a new inspiration on the campaign trail—her granddaughter, Charlotte Clinton Mezvinsky. While Clinton, widely seen as a likely 2016 presidential candidate, has not brought her only grandchild to political events, she has mentioned her several times in speeches in the four weeks since Charlotte was born. Today, at a rally for New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, Clinton told the crowd, according to Buzzfeed’s Ruby Cramer, ‘There is something about a new life in your family that really does focus you on the future, doesn’t it?’ The former Secretary of State attended a Women for Cuomo campaign event in New York, where she again referenced her granddaughter while advocating for Governor Cuomo’s reelection. Meanwhile, Chelsea Clinton, her husband Mark Mezvinsky, and their baby Charlotte have been photographed leaving Lenox Hill Hospital and later seen out in New York City. Chelsea was also spotted with friends about two and a half weeks after Charlotte’s birth. Clinton started incorporating mentions of her granddaughter into her speeches as early as five days after Charlotte was born on September 26. Speaking at a women-focused real estate convention in Miami on October 2, Clinton said, ‘I think my granddaughter has just as much God-given potential as a boy who was born in that hospital on the same day. I just believe that. That’s the way I was raised.’ This was not the first time Clinton mentioned Charlotte at a political event. At a recent rally for Pennsylvania gubernatorial candidate Tom Wolf, she stated, ‘You should not have to be the grandchild of a president to get a good education, to get good healthcare. Let’s make sure we give every child in Pennsylvania the same chance that I’m determined to give my granddaughter.’ Cramer reported that Clinton called Cuomo ‘the right leader at the right time with the right plan’ for New York, noting, ‘It’s not just because I’ve known Andrew Cuomo for a long time. It is because I’m now a grandmother.’ Cuomo, who has also been speculated as a possible presidential contender, thanked Clinton warmly and suggested he hopes she makes a major move in the future. After Clinton’s speech, at least two dozen people left the event, though Clinton stayed until the end, greeting supporters. At the rally, Clinton and Cuomo greeted their supporters, with Clinton repeating her support for Cuomo as the ‘right leader at the right time with the right plan’ for New York. The crowd enthusiastically cheered Clinton, shouting, ‘2016’ and ‘We love you Hillary!’ Clinton has said she will announce her political plans after the midterm elections, likely at the beginning of the new year. She has noted that one reason she might delay announcing another presidential campaign is to spend time experiencing life as a grandparent. Clinton told Charlie Rose on PBS in July, ‘I want to see what that feels like... I want to really be present, as I meet this new person in our family.’ She acknowledged that serving as Commander in Chief is a demanding role and said, ‘I just have to decide whether or not that’s what I want to do at this point in my life. It’s a very personal choice.’

article_content: The Sri Lankan government announced Thursday that its forces have made further advances into territory held by ethnic Tamil Tiger rebels, following the capture of the rebels' command center in the north. Sri Lankan workers recently buried the bodies of about 38 suspected Tamil Tiger fighters killed during recent clashes. The defense ministry's statement, which was also reported by the country's Lankapuvath national news agency, could not be independently confirmed. According to the agency, military jets bombed a rebel 'transit camp' in the Mullaittivu district on Wednesday evening. The defense ministry also alleged that rebels were firing at and killing civilians who attempted to flee the fighting. 'Facing defeat, LTTE terrorists are orchestrating a civilian tragedy,' the ministry stated on its website. The LTTE, or Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam—also known as the Tamil Tigers—have been fighting for an independent homeland for Sri Lanka's Tamil minority since 1983, in a civil war that has claimed more than 65,000 lives. In recent days, government forces have made significant progress in reclaiming rebel-held areas. Earlier this month, troops regained control of the northern town of Elephant Pass, a strategic gateway connecting mainland Sri Lanka with the Jaffna peninsula, which had been in rebel hands for over nine years. Its recapture enabled the government to resume ground transportation of troops and supplies along the highway linking the mainland to Jaffna, which previously required transport by air and sea.

La recuperación permitió al gobierno reanudar el transporte terrestre de tropas y suministros por la carretera hacia Jaffna, que antes solo podía hacerse por aire y mar.

LYON, France: New Zealand’s All Blacks confidently celebrated their dominant 96-17 victory over Italy in last week’s Rugby World Cup match. However, a 10-minute stretch early in the second half highlighted some concerns within the team. With a commanding 49-3 lead at halftime, New Zealand allowed Italy to score a try soon after the break, compounded by a flurry of All Black penalties. The team quickly regained control, ultimately scoring 14 tries and moving closer to a quarter-final spot ahead of their last Pool A match against Uruguay.

“It’s just great to see the All Black machine go out and do its business,” scrum coach Greg Feek told reporters Monday. “But you would have noticed, just after halftime, we got a bit sloppy. We thought our discipline was really good in that first half and then just for a little part there, we slipped off. We probably weren’t up to our standards, so that’s been a bit of a focus for us.”

Discipline has been a recurring issue for New Zealand, who had already conceded multiple penalties and yellow cards in their previous three matches, including their 71-3 win over Namibia. “We strive to find ways to get better, and so four penalties in 10 minutes probably isn’t good enough from us. We want to limit errors,” Feek added. “If you’re going to keep building your performances, and that’s what it’s about, we are more focused on performance than just on the 14 tries or the big win.”

With many players in strong form and the squad fully fit, Feek said the coaching staff—selectors Ian Foster, Joe Schmidt, and Jason Ryan—faced a tough decision picking the side for Thursday’s match against Uruguay. “I was looking at training footage the other day, and the players are training really well, including those who didn’t play on the weekend,” he added. “So Foz, Joe and Jase will have a few Panadols to try to put a team together.”

Sin embargo, un tramo de 10 minutos al comenzar la segunda mitad generó algunas preocupaciones dentro del equipo. Con una ventaja contundente de 49-3 al descanso, Nueva Zelanda permitió que Italia anotara un try poco después de reanudarse el juego, agravado por una serie de penales cometidos por los All Blacks. El equipo recuperó rápidamente el control, marcando finalmente 14 tries y acercándose a los cuartos de final antes de su último partido del Grupo A frente a Uruguay.

“Es genial ver a la máquina All Black haciendo lo suyo”, dijo el entrenador de scrum Greg Feek a periodistas el lunes. “Pero seguro notaron que, justo después del entretiempo, bajamos un poco el ritmo. Pensamos que nuestra disciplina fue muy buena en la primera mitad y luego, por un momento, nos relajamos. Probablemente no estuvimos a nuestro nivel habitual, así que eso ha sido un foco de atención para nosotros.”

La disciplina ha sido un problema recurrente para Nueva Zelanda, que ya había concedido múltiples penales y tarjetas amarillas en sus tres partidos anteriores, incluida la victoria por 71-3 contra Namibia. “Buscamos la forma de mejorar y, así que cuatro penales en 10 minutos probablemente no son lo suficientemente buenos para nosotros. Queremos limitar los errores”, agregó Feek. “Si queremos seguir mejorando nuestro rendimiento, y de eso se trata, estamos más enfocados en el desempeño que solo en los 14 tries o en la gran victoria.”

Con muchos jugadores en gran forma y el plantel completamente disponible, Feek comentó que los entrenadores –los seleccionadores Ian Foster, Joe Schmidt y Jason Ryan– se enfrentarán a una dura decisión al armar el equipo para el partido del jueves frente a Uruguay. “Vi algunos videos del entrenamiento el otro día y los jugadores están trabajando muy bien, incluyendo los que no jugaron el fin de semana”, añadió. “Así que Foz, Joe y Jase seguro necesitarán algunos analgésicos para elegir el equipo.”

article_content: Beneath Somerset’s Cheddar Gorge, explorers have discovered Britain’s largest cave chamber, now called The Frozen Deep. Inside, they found a huge muddy space scattered with giant boulders, made visible for the first time through Gavin Newman’s expert photography. The chamber features a striking 20-foot white stalactite—the country’s longest. The Frozen Deep is located at the end of the Reservoir Hole cave system, explored since 1951. For years, cavers were stopped by a rockfall blocking the main passage, known as the Grand Gallery, although persistent airflow suggested more space lay beyond. In 2008, retired doctor and experienced caver Pete Glanvill led a team using specialized tools and scaffolding to search for a route past several false leads. This year, after navigating a tight section referred to as ‘Hard Times,’ the team reached an immense open space they named Resurrection. From a passage about 30 feet above, the explorers finally entered The Frozen Deep, waiting for Glanvill to return from holiday so the team could descend together. Crossing the chamber can take up to ten minutes, along marked paths that help preserve the unique crystals and mud floor. The chamber covers almost 32,300 square feet—enough to fit six naves of Wells Cathedral—and has a volume of nearly 1.4 million cubic feet. Further exploration continues. At its lowest point, a stream flows into a muddy tunnel called Dingley Dell, leading to an underwater passage. Early dives indicate this could connect with Cheddar’s elusive ‘lost river,’ the River Yeo, which surfaces at the gorge’s base. Team member Martin Grass believes soon they may access new parts of the river and link The Frozen Deep to additional underground chambers stretching beneath the Mendip Hills, possibly unveiling one of Europe’s largest cave networks.

La cámara destaca por una impresionante estalactita blanca de 6 metros, la más larga del país. The Frozen Deep se ubica al final del sistema de cuevas Reservoir Hole, explorado desde 1951. Durante años, los espeleólogos no pudieron avanzar más allá de un derrumbe que bloqueaba el túnel principal, conocido como la Gran Galería, aunque una corriente de aire constante sugería que había más espacios ocultos. Este año, tras superar un tramo estrecho apodado ‘Hard Times’, el equipo llegó a una gran cavidad que llamaron Resurrection. Desde un pasaje situado a unos 9 metros sobre el suelo, los exploradores lograron finalmente entrar a The Frozen Deep, esperando el regreso de Glanvill de sus vacaciones para descender todos juntos. Cruzar la cámara puede llevar hasta diez minutos, siguiendo senderos marcados para proteger los cristales únicos y el delicado suelo de barro. La cavidad ocupa casi 3,000 metros cuadrados—lo suficiente para albergar seis naves de la catedral de Wells—y su volumen se aproxima a los 40,000 metros cúbicos. La exploración sigue adelante. En el punto más bajo, una corriente fluye hacia un túnel fangoso llamado Dingley Dell que lleva a un pasadizo sumergido. Immersiones preliminares sugieren que podría conectar con el esquivo ‘río perdido’ de Cheddar, el río Yeo, que surge en la base de la garganta. article_content: If you find yourself trekking through snowy Swiss woods, it's wise to take large steps—something I learned the hard way when I toppled face-first into a snow drift. Before I could recover, someone had already snapped a photo and spread it on social media. My attempt to get help from Beau, our towering cameraman, only resulted in more laughter. This sums up the whirlwind experience of attending the World Economic Forum in Davos for the first time. Longtime attendees like CNN’s Richard Quest (in his tenth year) delight in warning rookies that this gathering is both draining and expensive, but truly unparalleled. Davos itself is transformed into a fortress during the forum, with overpriced shops, high security, and a guest list packed with influential figures from business, politics, and academia. Everything costs a fortune—twenty dollars won’t even net you a simple meal—and no matter which language you try, you’re likely to be met with amusement. Even choosing the right shoes for the ever-changing conditions feels impossible. As the Scottish comedian Billy Connolly once put it: 'There's no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong kind of clothing.' In Davos, everyone seems to change outfits constantly, switching between overheated venues and icy streets. One business leader quickly ditched his fancy shoes for moon boots, while my budget gear held up—so far. Outside the closed-off zone, tourists get shuffled out as global journalists occupy the lodges and budget hotels. Local businesses give way to glitzy corporate events; in one weekend a pet shop became Barclays’ hospitality suite, and the RBS lounge looked more like an upscale bar than a bank. Getting into the event itself means passing through multiple layers of security and ending up at the Kongress Centre—reached via a quirky tunnel that looks more like a set from a sci-fi movie than a conference entrance. Once inside, your badge color determines your status—some grant better food and access than others, with journalists’ badges ranking low on the totem pole. It’s a modern-day class system, and navigating it isn’t easy. In an attempt to showcase the flood of research released for WEF, I set up a playful demonstration in the forest. Battling freezing wind and fumbling with a washing line for surveys, I remembered Richard’s helpful advice—ignore at your own risk: 'Don’t forget the long johns.' Ultimately, the real question remains: will the powerful people gathering at Davos do anything meaningful about global inequality, or will it all just pass by?
translated_content: Si alguna vez te encuentras caminando por los bosques nevados de Suiza, es mejor dar pasos largos, algo que aprendí por las malas cuando caí de cara en un montón de nieve. Antes de poder levantarme, alguien ya había tomado una foto y la compartió en las redes sociales. Mi intento de pedir ayuda a Beau, nuestro enorme camarógrafo, solo provocó más risas. Esto resume la experiencia de asistir al Foro Económico Mundial en Davos por primera vez. Veteranos como Richard Quest de CNN (en su décimo año) se divierten advirtiendo a los novatos que este evento es agotador y costoso, pero realmente no tiene igual. Davos se convierte en una fortaleza durante el foro, con tiendas carísimas, alta seguridad y una lista de invitados llena de figuras influyentes de los negocios, la política y la academia. Todo cuesta una fortuna—veinte dólares ni siquiera alcanzan para una comida sencilla—y no importa en qué idioma lo intentes, probablemente te recibirán con una sonrisa burlona. Incluso elegir los zapatos adecuados para las condiciones cambiantes es difícil. Como dijo el humorista escocés Billy Connolly: 'No existe el mal clima, sólo la ropa incorrecta.' En Davos, la gente parece cambiarse todo el tiempo, alternando entre espacios sobrecalentados y calles heladas. Un directivo cambió rápidamente sus zapatos elegantes por unas botas de nieve, mientras mi equipo económico hasta ahora ha aguantado. Fuera de la zona cerrada, los turistas desaparecen y los periodistas de todo el mundo ocupan hostales y hoteles baratos. Los negocios locales dan paso a glamurosos eventos corporativos; en un fin de semana, una tienda de mascotas se convirtió en la sala de hospitalidad de Barclays y el lounge de RBS parecía un bar elegante más que un banco. Entrar al evento implica superar varias capas de seguridad y llegar al Kongress Centre—a través de un túnel curioso que más parece salido de una película de ciencia ficción que la entrada a un congreso. Una vez adentro, el color de tu acreditación determina tu estatus—algunas dan acceso a mejor comida y zonas, mientras que las de periodista están entre las de menor rango. Es como un sistema de clases moderno, y navegarlo no es nada fácil. Para mostrar la avalancha de informes que se publican para el WEF, monté una demostración divertida en el bosque. Peleando contra el viento helado y luchando con una cuerda para colgar encuestas, recordé el valioso consejo de Richard—ignóralo bajo tu propio riesgo: 'No te olvides de la ropa interior larga.' Al final, la gran pregunta sigue siendo: ¿harán algo realmente importante los poderosos que se reúnen en Davos para combatir la desigualdad global, o el evento simplemente pasará de largo?

article_content: Red Bull team principal Christian Horner stated that it would have been 'wrong' to impose team orders on Sebastian Vettel and Daniel Ricciardo during the Singapore Grand Prix. Vettel and Ricciardo were running second and third behind race winner Lewis Hamilton in the final laps at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. Horner could have asked them to swap positions but chose not to. Ricciardo started the race 72 points behind Nico Rosberg, who retired early due to a wiring loom failure in his steering wheel. Daniel Ricciardo finished third, ending the race 60 points behind Hamilton. With team orders, this gap could have been reduced to 57. With double points awarded at the season's final race in Abu Dhabi and given Mercedes’ ongoing reliability issues, Ricciardo’s championship chances remain in play. Despite this, Horner said: 'Both mathematically have a chance, even though it's a long shot. So it's down to them racing each other on the track. It would be wrong to interfere in that situation.' After the previous race in Italy, Ricciardo suggested it might help him if the team began to favor him. Lewis Hamilton won the Singapore Grand Prix. Daniel Ricciardo took third, while Sebastian Vettel finished second. Reigning four-time champion Vettel is now 117 points behind, with 150 points still available. Horner added: 'Daniel is totally comfortable and happy with the situation. If there were a realistic chance of Daniel winning and Sebastian was mathematically out of the championship then we'd do what’s best for the team. But as I say, at the moment, it's a long shot.' Mercedes continues to lead, but their reliability remains an issue. Ricciardo could still contend if Mercedes faces further problems. Horner concluded: 'Mercedes have an enormous advantage at this point, but we'll take it one race at a time. Both are still just in it and both have taken points from Nico. Daniel conceded three points to Seb, but will that be decisive? That's impossible to know right now. At the moment, it doesn't make sense to interfere with team orders.'

article_content: A devastating 6.3 magnitude earthquake recently struck western Afghanistan, killing over 2,000 people and injuring around 10,000, though the real numbers may be higher. Rescue efforts are hindered as teams and volunteers must search through rubble with minimal equipment, often relying on shovels or their bare hands. Sabir, an aid worker in Herat province, highlighted the desperate situation, expressing fears that a lack of appropriate rescue tools and trained teams will cause further loss of life. He and others are pleading for urgent international assistance, as Afghanistan's disaster response capacity is severely limited, especially since the 2021 Taliban takeover, which led to reduced resources and loss of skilled workers. Zenda Jan district in Herat has been especially devastated, with at least 13 villages suffering severe damage—nine nearly erased. Entire communities have been reduced to ruins, and volunteers are left to search for survivors among the devastation. Sabir described waking up in terror during the quake. After ensuring his family's safety, he joined rescue efforts, finding widespread destruction and many people, including children and the elderly, either missing or dead. There is an urgent shortfall of food, clean water, and shelter, particularly for women and children. Volunteers have brought some aid, but the need for basic supplies, medical help, and psychological assistance—especially for orphaned or separated children—is far greater. Disaster management expert Abdul Baset Rahmani noted that the situation exceeds the capabilities of local authorities and emphasized the pressing need for modern rescue equipment and international aid. Despite these daunting challenges, rescuers remain determined to save more lives. In one village of nearly 2,000 people, only 40 survivors have been found so far, with many others still missing. Even so, moments of hope persist, like when a man was pulled out alive from under the rubble—the only survivor in his family. Volunteers continue their efforts, hoping to find more survivors amid the ruins.

Los esfuerzos de rescate se ven obstaculizados, ya que los equipos y voluntarios deben buscar entre los escombros con equipo mínimo, muchas veces usando solo palas o sus propias manos. Sabir, un trabajador humanitario en la provincia de Herat, señaló la situación desesperada y expresó temor de que la falta de herramientas adecuadas y equipos entrenados cause más pérdidas de vidas. Él y otros piden ayuda internacional urgente, ya que la capacidad de respuesta ante desastres en Afganistán es muy limitada, especialmente desde que los talibanes retomaron el poder en 2021, lo que redujo recursos y provocó la salida de personal calificado. El distrito de Zenda Jan en Herat ha sido especialmente devastado, con al menos 13 aldeas gravemente dañadas—nueve casi completamente destruidas. Comunidades enteras quedaron reducidas a escombros, y los voluntarios deben buscar sobrevivientes entre la destrucción. Sabir relató que se despertó aterrado durante el sismo. Tras asegurar la seguridad de su familia, se unió a las labores de rescate, encontrando destrucción masiva y a muchas personas, incluidos niños y ancianos, desaparecidas o fallecidas. Hay una escasez urgente de alimentos, agua y refugio, especialmente para mujeres y niños. Los voluntarios han proporcionado algo de ayuda, pero la necesidad de suministros básicos, asistencia médica y apoyo psicológico—sobre todo para niños huérfanos o separados de sus familias—es mucho mayor. El experto en gestión de desastres Abdul Baset Rahmani advirtió que la situación supera la capacidad de las autoridades locales y destacó la necesidad urgente de equipos modernos de rescate y ayuda internacional. A pesar de estos grandes desafíos, los rescatistas siguen decididos a salvar más vidas. article_content:
Lendlease Group and Alphabet's Google have mutually agreed to end their development services agreements for four master-planned districts, valued at $15 billion, in the San Francisco Bay Area, according to an announcement from the Australian company on Friday. This decision comes as developers continue to withdraw from California's real estate market.

In 2019, Lendlease was awarded a contract by Google to develop residential and retail spaces in Sunnyvale, San Jose, and Mountain View. The project aimed to add about 15,000 new housing units to the region. California's commercial real estate market is among the hardest hit globally, with reduced demand for office space due to increased remote work and declining property values. Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield, which owns one of San Francisco's largest shopping centers, has also opted to exit the market.

Lendlease was slated to develop up to 15 million square feet of residential, retail, and hospitality space, while Google would handle office space development. "We have been optimizing our real estate investments in the Bay Area, and part of that process involves exploring various options to advance our development projects and fulfill our housing commitment," said Alexa Arena, senior director of development at Google. As of the end of June, 12,900 of the planned housing units had received development approval in San Jose and Mountain View, according to Google. A company spokesperson noted that Google is still seeking collaboration with developers and investment partners to move Bay Area developments forward.

Earlier this year, Lendlease also paused its 47-story Hayes Point project in central San Francisco—its largest investment in the Americas—while seeking tenants or co-investors. Lendlease stated it would remove the San Francisco Bay project, which was expected to begin construction in the 2026 fiscal year, from its development pipeline. "While market expectations for the project had decreased over the past 12 to 18 months, this change negatively affects medium-term (FY26-28) earnings," said analysts at UBS. However, Lendlease maintained its financial forecast for fiscal 2024, expecting its core operating return on equity to remain at the lower end of the 8 to 10 percent range.

article_content: Electricity pylons are often seen as unsightly landmarks that tower over the landscape, though some online communities see them as uniquely beautiful. As the UK expands its use of renewable energy, there are concerns that local opposition could slow the government’s plans to build new power lines. To address resistance, Chancellor Jeremy Hunt is expected to announce that households living near new pylons and substations may get up to £1,000 a year off their energy bills. Some believe redesigning pylons to be more attractive might change public opinion. In 2008, US-based architects Choi + Shine proposed the ‘Land of Giants’ project, featuring giant human-shaped pylons. Jin Choi said the idea came from watching rows of pylons along the road and imagining them as moving giants. Her collaborator, Thomas Shine, argues that infrastructure can be designed to be beautiful, not just functional. Despite winning a design competition in Iceland, these giant artistic pylons have not been built anywhere. The materials are standard but assembled differently, and sometimes political disagreements arise over their location. Proposals for these pylons have also appeared in Norway, New Mexico, Georgia, and Chile. Jin Choi expressed some frustration about the designs not being constructed, but she remains hopeful. Other efforts to make pylons less intrusive include artistic transformations, like the one in Essen, Germany in 2010. Alternatively, some utilities have tried camouflaging infrastructure, such as a phone mast by Three in South Queensferry, Scotland, designed to look like a tree. Community reactions were mixed, with some locals criticizing its look. Disguising all pylons would likely be expensive and impractical. Instead, the National Grid and the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) held a competition in 2011 to redesign pylons, leading to Danish architect Bystrup’s ‘T-pylon’ design. T-pylons are shorter and faster to install than traditional models. The first T-pylons were energised earlier this year between Bridgwater and Loxton in Somerset. Some residents compared them to Pat Butcher’s earrings, MC Hammer, and a contraceptive coil. National Grid reported that most people preferred T-pylons over conventional lattice designs. Another way to make pylons more acceptable is to compensate those living nearby. Ireland provides payments between €2,000 and €30,000 to people living within 200 meters of new power lines. Energy expert Nick Winser’s report to the UK government recommended this model, stating that compensation costs less than routing cables underground. Ultimately, while some focus on new designs or compensation, others encourage people to appreciate pylons as they are. Kevin Mosedale, who runs the ‘Pylon of the Month’ blog, acknowledges why people might dislike them but also celebrates their distinctive appearance, referencing Jonathan Glancey’s description of their ‘gaunt skeletal beauty’.
translated_content: Las torres eléctricas suelen considerarse monumentos poco atractivos que dominan el paisaje, aunque algunas comunidades en línea las ven con una belleza particular. A medida que el Reino Unido aumenta el uso de energías renovables, preocupa que la oposición local pueda retrasar los planes del gobierno para construir nuevas líneas eléctricas. Para enfrentar esa resistencia, se prevé que el ministro de Hacienda, Jeremy Hunt, anuncie que los hogares cerca de nuevas torres y subestaciones eléctricas podrían recibir hasta £1,000 al año de descuento en sus facturas de energía. Algunos creen que rediseñar las torres para hacerlas más atractivas podría cambiar la opinión pública. En 2008, los arquitectos estadounidenses Choi + Shine propusieron el proyecto 'Land of Giants', con torres eléctricas en forma de gigantes humanos. Jin Choi contó que la idea surgió al observar filas de torres en la carretera e imaginarlas como gigantes en movimiento. Su colega, Thomas Shine, sostiene que la infraestructura también puede ser bella, no solo funcional. A pesar de haber ganado un concurso de diseño en Islandia, estas torres artísticas aún no se han construido en ningún lugar. Los materiales son convencionales pero ensamblados de otra forma, y a veces surgen disputas políticas sobre su ubicación. Ha habido propuestas similares en Noruega, Nuevo México, Georgia y Chile. Jin Choi manifestó cierta frustración por la falta de construcciones, pero sigue optimista. Otras iniciativas para suavizar el impacto visual de las torres incluyen intervenciones artísticas, como la de Essen, Alemania, en 2010. También algunas empresas han intentado camuflar infraestructuras, como una antena de Three en South Queensferry, Escocia, diseñada para parecer un árbol. Las opiniones de la comunidad fueron divididas, y algunos la criticaron por su apariencia. Disfrazar todas las torres sería costoso y poco práctico. Por eso National Grid y el Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) realizaron en 2011 un concurso para rediseñar torres, lo que llevó al 'T-pylon' del arquitecto danés Bystrup. Los T-pylon son más bajos y rápidos de instalar que los modelos tradicionales. Los primeros se energizaron este año entre Bridgwater y Loxton en Somerset. Algunos residentes los compararon con los pendientes de Pat Butcher, MC Hammer y un dispositivo anticonceptivo. National Grid informó que la mayoría prefiere estos diseños ante los clásicos de celosía. Otra estrategia es compensar a quienes viven cerca de torres eléctricas. Irlanda otorga entre €2,000 y €30,000 a quienes viven a menos de 200 metros de nuevas líneas. El experto energético Nick Winser recomendó este modelo en el Reino Unido, afirmando que esta compensación cuesta mucho menos que enterrar los cables. Al final, aunque algunos prefieren los nuevos diseños o recibir pagos, otros optan por apreciar las torres como son. Kevin Mosedale, creador del blog 'Pylon of the Month', entiende las reservas, pero también celebra su aspecto particular, citando a Jonathan Glancey y su definición de 'belleza esquelética y austera'.

Afghan farmers have lost over USD 1 billion in income following the Taliban’s ban on poppy cultivation, according to a United Nations drugs agency report released Sunday. Before the ban, Afghanistan was the world’s leading opium producer and a major source of heroin for Europe and Asia. The Taliban, after coming to power in August 2021, pledged to eradicate the country’s drug industry and imposed a formal ban in April 2022. This decision severely affected hundreds of thousands of farmers and laborers who relied on opium production for their livelihoods.

According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), opium cultivation in Afghanistan fell by 95% after the ban. Up until 2023, Afghanistan’s opiate exports often surpassed the value of its legal exports, accounting for 9-14% of the national GDP. UN officials caution that the sharp decline of the opium economy is likely to have profound, far-reaching impacts on the country.

UNODC executive director Ghada Waly stated, "Afghans need urgent humanitarian assistance to meet their immediate needs, absorb the shock of lost income, and save lives." She emphasized the need for strong investment in sustainable livelihoods to offer Afghans alternatives to opium cultivation.

Currently, Afghanistan is grappling with drought, severe economic hardship, and the lingering effects of decades of conflict and natural disasters. The loss of opium income, along with the cessation of international financial support that sustained the previous government’s economy, is driving many Afghans into poverty, hunger, and addiction.

A UNODC report from September indicated that Afghanistan has become the world’s fastest-growing producer of methamphetamine, with seizures of the synthetic drug rising as poppy cultivation shrinks. The agency warns that falling incomes along the opiate supply chain could encourage other illegal activities, such as trafficking in arms, people, or synthetic drugs.

article_content: Two airplanes made contact on the ground at Newark Liberty International Airport last night, just before takeoff. According to Federal Aviation Administration officials, no injuries occurred during the collision, which happened around 7:30pm at one of the nation's busiest airports. The left wing of a Scandinavian Airlines Airbus A330 clipped the tail of an ExpressJet, operating as United Express, while both aircraft were on the taxiway. Scandinavian Airlines Flight 908, bound for Oslo, was behind ExpressJet Flight 4226, headed to Nashville, when the incident took place as the Scandinavian Airlines plane was turning onto another taxiway. Both planes returned to their gates—the ExpressJet was towed, and passengers on both aircraft disembarked safely. All 31 passengers from the ExpressJet flight were re-accommodated. The Federal Aviation Administration is currently investigating the accident. ExpressJet released a statement saying it was cooperating with officials to determine the cause. Scandinavian Airlines, which serves as a hub carrier for Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, had not immediately commented. Newark Liberty International Airport, opened in 1928, is the nation's oldest airfield and home to the first commercial airline terminal in the United States.
